newsitem.title: USA: Albright heads for Moscow to push NATO charter.
newsitem.headline: Albright heads for Moscow to push NATO charter.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright leaves for Moscow on Wednesday hoping to push forward talks on a NATO-Russia pact to soothe Kremlin fears over the entry of East European states to the Western alliance.
Albright will hold discussions on Thursday with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov during a visit lasting little more than 24 hours.

In deference to NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who has been leading the negotiations for NATO, U.S. officials said they did not expect Albright's visit to clinch a deal. Solana is due to meet Primakov in Luxembourg on May 6.
But the officials said Albright would seek to make progress on the roadblocks still holding up agreement on the charter both sides want to sign in late May.

That would be more than a month before a Madrid summit at which NATO will announce the first former Warsaw Pact countries to be invited to join -- almost certainly the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, and possibly one or two others.

To soften long-standing Russian opposition to the plan, NATO agreed with Moscow last December to start talks on a charter that would give the Kremlin the right to close consultations with the alliance on European security questions.
Although Russian President Boris Yeltsin has confidently predicted the charter will be signed in Paris on May 27, Western officials have been more cautious, saying problems remain to be ironed out.
The main obstacle is Russia's demand for binding guarantees that NATO will never station nuclear arms or outside troops on the territory of new members, something NATO refuses to give.
"We will not compromise on this issue," Albright told the Senate Armed Services Committee last week.

"All we have done and all we will do is to restate unilaterally existing NATO policy: that in the current and foreseeable security environment, we have no plan, no need and no intention to station nuclear weapons in the new member countries, nor do we contemplate permanently stationing substantial combat forces."
U.S. officials say one circumstance in which NATO might want to go back on that promise would be if Russia stationed nuclear weapons on the territory of other ex-Soviet republics.

The Washington Post said on Wednesday that Russia might have been encouraged to push for greater concessions by assurances it received from NATO's senior military officer, Gen. Klaus Naumann, during a visit to Moscow in late March.

The newspaper quoted U.S. officials and Western diplomats as saying Naumann gave the Russians some informal assurances about NATO's nuclear planning that went significantly beyond anything NATO was prepared to put in writing.
Russian leaders have built up to Albright's visit with a barrage of rhetoric against NATO expansion.

"I am convinced that NATO's expansion to the East is a gross political error by the West. It is not in the West's interests and it is certainly not in Russia's interests. It's in the interests of extremists," First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais told the Kommersant Daily newspaper on Tuesday.

Primakov met Albright's deputy Strobe Talbott in Moscow on Wednesday, and the Russian foreign ministry said he was still insisting that NATO "make more concrete" its pledges on not moving NATO structures eastwards.

Despite the differences, U.S. officials say the Russian- speaking Albright has good relations with Primakov. They said she was not expected to see Yeltsin, who is on vacation in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright might conclude her visit by meeting Russian intellectuals and academics on Friday.
